Being a ruler over a group of people is marked with stress, hard decisions, and sleepless nights—certainly not a position for the mentally weak or immature. The position is difficult, be it sheriff, mayor, governor, or president. The average person does not fully mature until the age of 25, according to neuroscientific studies.1 And yet, in AD 54, a ruler was appointed who was only seventeen years old. This was no petty judge or political secretary. He was crowned ruler over one of the largest empires of the world at that time. The boy’s name was Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus—commonly called Nero. He was the fifth emperor of Rome.

Nero was not brought into power by any election or choice of his citizens. His mother, Agrippina, had married Caesar Claudius (her uncle), emperor of Rome. Claudius adopted Nero as his son. Nero would go on to marry Claudius’ daughter Octavia, his own cousin and stepsister.

On October 13, A.D. 54, Agrippina poisoned her powerful husband, and her son Nero became emperor. It was rumored that Nero and his mother had an incestuous relationship, but the new ruler was well received by his subjects and seemed eager to please them, ordering grand public buildings to be built, as well as lowering taxes and the price of food. However, it was not to last.

Nero soon killed his brother-in-law, who was fourteen, which angered his wife. At this point, the emperor was in a relationship with a freedwoman (a formerly enslaved person), so he had his wife exiled. When this sparked public outrage, he had Octavia beheaded on false charges of being unfaithful.

He then became infatuated with a woman named Poppaea Sabina, who was scheming to marry him. Sabina roused Nero to such fear and jealousy that he decided to kill his mother for fear of losing the throne. The plan was simple—while Agrippina was on a cruise ship, it would be discreetly sunk, and Nero’s mother would drown. However, this was not to be. Agrippina was a strong swimmer and escaped with her life. Undeterred, Nero dispatched his executioners to stab her to death in broad daylight. Unfortunately, things had just gotten started for the most powerful man in the empire and these bizarre and inhuman acts were only a sampling of what was to come.

Nero was given to fits of rage and became violent towards his wife in one such outburst. He kicked Sabina repeatedly until both she and her unborn child died. Nero is said to have regretted this, and he soon started a hunt for anyone who looked like Sabina, his dead wife. He finally found a slave that is said to have resembled her strongly, and they were married. The catch? The slave was a man. Nero took to dressing him in the clothing of a woman and referring to him as a lady. At this point, Nero’s slippery slope was only getting more slippery. He believed himself to be an artist—a genius, even—and gave massive public performances. If you were in attendance, you could not leave. Why? The doors were locked. Nero also dreamed of singing to his enemies and bringing them to tears for their perceived wrongdoings.

But the emperor was not content with only putting on musical performances. In A.D. 67, he entered into the Olympic Games, which was against the rules (no emperor was allowed to compete in the Games). Nevertheless, Nero entered. He introduced new competitions, such as trumpeting and acting. He entered into several and won each one. His actions caused much outrage since the Olympics were considered a sacred event and Nero had changed them.

However, Nero had an even bigger goal in mind. The chariot races were the biggest spectacle the Olympics had to offer. In them, chariot riders were allowed a team of four horses. Teams would race around a massive arena for a total of seven laps. Sometimes wheels fell off, or chariots crashed into each other. It was not uncommon for drivers to be thrown from their ride and to be trampled to death or to be dragged by their own team of horses. However, the winner would be celebrated and highly paid.

Knowing all the difficulty, danger, and stress involved, you can only imagine how the charioteers felt to see Emperor Nero roll up to the racetrack in an expensive chariot and a team consisting of not four, but ten horses. As it turns out, Nero was inexperienced and out of shape. Almost immediately, he lost control of his team and was thrown from the chariot, being seriously injured in the process. Despite never finishing the race, Nero won first place.

This incident does a good job of demonstrating Nero’s attitude toward his authority at this point in his reign. In fact, in A.D. 66, he won more than 1,800 first-place prizes for his supposed exhibits of artistry. Here was a man that could not be told “no”.

On the night of July 18, A.D. 64, a fire started in Rome’s Circus Maximus. The fire grew and spread, becoming out of control. The fire would rage for the next six days, leaving almost no part of the city untouched. It was devastating for the citizens of Rome and would go on to be the incident Nero would be most widely known for. Many ancient writers blamed Nero for starting the fire, although he was not in the city when it began. Whether or not he started the fire, Nero needed someone to blame. He chose a group of people who were despised and feared by the Romans and tortured them relentlessly. That group was known as the Christians. Tacitus, a secular Roman writer, described it as such, “Nero fastened the guilt and inflicted the most exquisite tortures on a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace. Mockery of every sort was added to their deaths. Covered with the skins of beasts, they were torn by dogs and perished, or were nailed to crosses, or were doomed to the flames and burnt, to serve as nightly illumination when daylight had expired.”

Meanwhile, Nero grew even more wicked. He ruthlessly slaughtered Christian men, women, and children, and plunged ever deeper into immorality. Finally, On June 9, AD 68, Nero, the last emperor of Rome killed himself after having been declared a public enemy by the Roman Senate. He was only 31 years old.

So, here is a man corrupt in every way. His lifestyle was deeply offensive to Christianity, and his persecution was one of the most horrible in history. How would we respond to such a ruler? How did Christians respond to him?

Paul lived under Nero’s reign. He saw all the horrible things detailed above. Yet, he gave the church the following admonition: Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation. For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same: For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. Wherefore ye must needs be subject, not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake –Romans 13: 1-5.

These words seem impossible when we consider the situation. Yet the Word of God tells us that our governmental authorities are put in place by God Himself. What a testimony! How much more, then, are we called to respect our authorities—to not slander them; to obey them in all possible aspects; to stay away from their elections and campaigns; and yet, to yield ourselves to God and His authority as our final say?! Or, as Paul put it, Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God… –Romans 13:1.

The believers of the early church saw Nero—the murderous, bloodthirsty, corrupt emperor—as a man ordained of God. They sought to honor and respect him in his authority, while ultimately yielding to the higher authority of God. Herein, we see a potential paradox, that the earthly authorities are “ministers of God” to be honored and obeyed, yet IF the time would come wherein the believer is required by the civil authorities to disobey God, we then have a higher responsibility—…We ought to obey God rather than men –Acts 5:29.

This all puts a great responsibility on our shoulders today as Christians living in an increasingly corrupt and evil society. Can we find that biblical balance between honoring our governmental leaders while still obeying God in all things? Or do we fail just like the unregenerate around us in picking apart the faults of our earthly authorities when we feel our “easy living” being trodden upon?

See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is –Ephesians 5:15-17. And Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful –1 Corinthians 4:2.

Let each one of us as committed, born-again, Bible-believing Christians walk circumspectly, redeeming the time. For we all want to be found faithful in that soon-coming day when we all will stand before the judgment seat to receive our just reward.

Ser gobernante de un grupo de personas está marcado por el estrés, decisiones difíciles y noches sin dormir—ciertamente no es un puesto para los mentalmente débiles o inmaduros. El cargo es difícil, ya sea alguacil, alcalde, gobernador o presidente. La persona promedio no madura por completo hasta la edad de 25 años, según estudios neurocientíficos.1 Y, sin embargo, en el año 54 d. C. se nombró a un gobernante que tenía solo diecisiete años. No se trataba de un juez menor ni de un secretario político. Fue coronado como gobernante de uno de los imperios más grandes del mundo en aquel tiempo. El nombre del joven era Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus—comúnmente llamado Nerón. Fue el quinto emperador de Roma.

Nerón no llegó al poder por elección ni por la decisión de sus conciudadanos. Su madre, Agripina, se había casado con el César Claudio (su tío), emperador de Roma. Claudio adoptó a Nerón como su hijo. Nerón contraería matrimonio con la hija de Claudio, Octavia, su propia prima y hermanastra.

El 13 de octubre del año 54 d. C., Agripina envenenó a su poderoso marido y su hijo Nerón se convirtió en emperador. Se rumoraba que Nerón y su madre mantenían una relación incestuosa, pero el nuevo gobernante fue bien recibido por sus súbditos y pareció ansioso por agradarles, ordenando la construcción de grandes edificios públicos, además de bajar impuestos y el precio de los alimentos. Sin embargo, eso no duraría.

Nerón pronto mató a su cuñado, que tenía catorce años, lo que enfureció a su esposa. En ese momento, el emperador mantenía una relación con una liberta (una persona anteriormente esclavizada), por lo que mandó exiliar a su esposa. Cuando esto provocó la indignación pública, hizo decapitar a Octavia con acusaciones falsas de infidelidad.

Luego se enamoró de una mujer llamada Poppaea Sabina, que conspiraba para casarse con él. Sabina despertó en Nerón tanto temor y celos que decidió matar a su madre por miedo a perder el trono. El plan era simple—mientras Agripina estaba en un barco de recreo, este se hundiría discretamente y la madre de Nerón se ahogaría. Sin embargo, esto no sucedió. Agripina era una buena nadadora y escapó con vida. Sin inmutarse, Nerón envió a sus ejecutores a apuñalarla hasta matarla en plena luz del día. Desgraciadamente, las cosas apenas habían comenzado para el hombre más poderoso del imperio y estos actos extraños e inhumanos fueron solo una muestra de lo que vendría.

Nerón sufrió arrebatos de ira y se volvió violento con su esposa en uno de esos estallidos. Pateó a Sabina repetidamente hasta que ella y su hijo no nacido murieron. Se dice que Nerón lamentó esto, y pronto comenzó una búsqueda de cualquiera que se pareciera a Sabina, su esposa muerta. Finalmente encontró a un esclavo que, según se decía, se le parecía mucho, y se casaron. ¿La trampa? El esclavo era un hombre. Nerón lo vestía con ropa de mujer y se refería a él como dama. En este punto, la pendiente resbaladiza de Nerón se volvía cada vez más traicionera. Se creía a sí mismo un artista—e incluso un genio—y ofrecía enormes espectáculos públicos. Si asistías, no podías marcharte. ¿Por qué? Las puertas estaban cerradas. Nerón también soñaba con cantar para sus enemigos y hacerlos llorar por los supuestos agravios cometidos en su contra.

Pero el emperador no se contentó con solo dar actuaciones musicales. En el año 67 d. C. participó en los Juegos Olímpicos, lo cual contravenía las reglas (ningún emperador podía competir en los Juegos). Sin embargo, Nerón participó. Introdujo nuevas competencias, como tocar la trompeta y la actuación. Compitió en varias y ganó en todas. Sus acciones causaron gran indignación, ya que los Olímpicos eran considerados un evento sagrado y Nerón los había cambiado.

No obstante, Nerón tenía una meta aún mayor en mente. Las carreras de carros eran el mayor espectáculo que ofrecían los Olímpicos. En ellas, los aurigas podían llevar un equipo de cuatro caballos. Los equipos daban una vuelta en una enorme arena por un total de siete vueltas. A veces las ruedas se desprendían o los carros se estrellaban entre sí. No era raro que los conductores fueran arrojados de su carro y pisoteados hasta la muerte o arrastrados por su propio equipo de caballos. Sin embargo, el vencedor era celebrado y pagado generosamente.

Sabiendo toda la dificultad, el peligro y el estrés implicados, solo puedes imaginar cómo se sintieron los aurigas al ver al emperador Nerón llegar a la pista en un carro caro y con un equipo formado no por cuatro, sino por diez caballos. Resultó que Nerón era inexperto y estaba fuera de forma. Casi de inmediato perdió el control de su equipo y fue arrojado del carro, resultando gravemente herido en el proceso. A pesar de no terminar la carrera, Nerón obtuvo el primer puesto.

Este incidente ilustra bien la actitud de Nerón hacia su autoridad en este punto de su reinado. De hecho, en el año 66 d. C. ganó más de 1.800 primeros premios por sus supuestas exhibiciones artísticas. Éste era un hombre al que no se le podía decir “no”.

La noche del 18 de julio del año 64 d. C., se inició un incendio en el Circo Máximo de Roma. El incendio creció y se propagó, saliéndose de control. El fuego ardería durante los siguientes seis días, dejando casi ninguna parte de la ciudad intacta. Fue devastador para los ciudadanos de Roma y pasaría a ser el incidente por el que Nerón sería más conocido. Muchos escritores antiguos lo acusaron de haber iniciado el incendio, aunque él no estaba en la ciudad cuando comenzó. Fuera o no responsable, Nerón necesitaba a alguien a quien culpar. Eligió a un grupo de personas despreciadas y temidas por los romanos y los torturó sin piedad. Ese grupo era conocido como los cristianos. Tácito, un escritor romano secular, lo describió así: “Nerón cargó la culpa y les infligió los supremos tormentos a una clase, odiada por sus atrocidades y llamada por el pueblo cristianos. A sus muertes se añadió todo tipo de escarnio. Cubriéndolos con pieles de animales, eran desgarrados por perros y perecían, o eran clavados en cruces, o condenados a las llamas y quemados, para servir de iluminación nocturna cuando expiraba la luz del día.”

Mientras tanto, Nerón se volvió aún más perverso. Masacró sin piedad a hombres, mujeres y niños cristianos y se hundió cada vez más en la inmoralidad. Finalmente, el 9 de junio del año 68 d. C., Nerón, el último emperador de Roma, se suicidó después de haber sido declarado enemigo público por el Senado romano. Tenía solo 31 años.

Así pues, aquí tenemos a un hombre corrompido en todos los sentidos. Su estilo de vida era profundamente ofensivo para el cristianismo, y su persecución fue una de las más horribles de la historia. ¿Cómo debíamos responder ante un gobernante así? ¿Cómo respondieron los cristianos ante él?

Pablo vivió bajo el reinado de Nerón. Vio todas las cosas horribles detalladas arriba. Sin embargo, dio a la iglesia la siguiente amonestación: Sométase toda persona a las autoridades superiores; porque no hay autoridad sino de parte de Dios, y las que hay, por Dios han sido establecidas. De modo que quien se opone a la autoridad, a lo establecido por Dios resiste; y los que resisten acarrean condenación para sí mismos. Porque los magistrados no están para infundir temor al que hace el bien, sino al malo. ¿Quieres, pues, no temer la autoridad? Haz lo bueno, y tendrás alabanza de ella; porque ella es ministro de Dios para tu bien. Mas si haces lo malo, teme; porque no en vano lleva la espada; pues es ministro de Dios, vengador para castigar al que hace lo malo. Por tanto, es necesario que le estéis sujetos, no solamente por razón de la ira, sino también por causa de la conciencia—Romanos 13:1-5.

Estas palabras parecen imposibles cuando consideramos la situación. Sin embargo, la Palabra de Dios nos dice que nuestras autoridades gubernamentales son puestas en su lugar por el mismo Dios. ¡Qué testimonio! ¡Cuánto más, entonces, estamos llamados a respetar a nuestras autoridades—no calumniarlas; obedecerlas en todo lo posible; mantenernos al margen de sus elecciones y campañas; y, sin embargo, someternos a Dios y a Su autoridad como nuestro veredicto final! ¿O, como lo expresó Pablo, Sométase toda persona a las autoridades superiores; porque no hay autoridad sino de parte de Dios…—Romanos 13:1?

Los creyentes de la iglesia primitiva vieron a Nerón—el emperador asesino, sanguinario y corrupto—como un hombre ordenado por Dios. Buscaron honrarle y respetar su autoridad, aunque en última instancia se sometían a la autoridad superior de Dios. Aquí vemos un posible paradoja: que las autoridades terrenales son “ministros de Dios” a quienes hay que honrar y obedecer, sin embargo, SI llegara el momento en que las autoridades civiles exigieran al creyente desobedecer a Dios, entonces tenemos una responsabilidad superior—Debemos obedecer a Dios antes que a los hombres—Hechos 5:29.

Todo esto pone sobre nuestros hombros hoy una gran responsabilidad como cristianos que vivimos en una sociedad cada vez más corrupta y malvada. ¿Podemos encontrar ese equilibrio bíblico entre honrar a nuestros líderes gubernamentales y, al mismo tiempo, obedecer a Dios en todas las cosas? ¿O fracasamos igual que los incrédulos que nos rodean al desmenuzar las faltas de nuestras autoridades terrenales cuando sentimos que pisotean nuestra “vida cómoda”?

Así que mirad con diligencia cómo andéis, no como necios sino como sabios, aprovechando bien el tiempo, porque los días son malos. Por tanto, no seáis insensatos, sino entendidos de cuál sea la voluntad del Señor—Efesios 5:15-17. Y Que cada uno nos tenga por servidores de Cristo, y administradores de los misterios de Dios. Ahora bien, se requiere de los administradores, que cada uno sea hallado fiel—1 Corintios 4:2.

Que cada uno de nosotros, como cristianos comprometidos, nacidos de nuevo y creyentes de la Biblia, andemos con prudencia, aprovechando el tiempo. Porque todos queremos ser hallados fieles en ese día venidero cuando todos compareceremos ante el tribunal para recibir nuestra justa recompensa.

Being a ruler over a group of people is marked with stress, hard decisions, and sleepless nights—certainly not a position for the mentally weak or immature. The position is difficult, be it sheriff, mayor, governor, or president. The average person does not fully mature until the age of 25, according to neuroscientific studies.1 And yet, in AD 54, a ruler was appointed who was only seventeen years old. This was no petty judge or political secretary. He was crowned ruler over one of the largest empires of the world at that time. The boy’s name was Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus—commonly called Nero. He was the fifth emperor of Rome.

Nero was not brought into power by any election or choice of his citizens. His mother, Agrippina, had married Caesar Claudius (her uncle), emperor of Rome. Claudius adopted Nero as his son. Nero would go on to marry Claudius’ daughter Octavia, his own cousin and stepsister.

On October 13, A.D. 54, Agrippina poisoned her powerful husband, and her son Nero became emperor. It was rumored that Nero and his mother had an incestuous relationship, but the new ruler was well received by his subjects and seemed eager to please them, ordering grand public buildings to be built, as well as lowering taxes and the price of food. However, it was not to last.

Nero soon killed his brother-in-law, who was fourteen, which angered his wife. At this point, the emperor was in a relationship with a freedwoman (a formerly enslaved person), so he had his wife exiled. When this sparked public outrage, he had Octavia beheaded on false charges of being unfaithful.

He then became infatuated with a woman named Poppaea Sabina, who was scheming to marry him. Sabina roused Nero to such fear and jealousy that he decided to kill his mother for fear of losing the throne. The plan was simple—while Agrippina was on a cruise ship, it would be discreetly sunk, and Nero’s mother would drown. However, this was not to be. Agrippina was a strong swimmer and escaped with her life. Undeterred, Nero dispatched his executioners to stab her to death in broad daylight. Unfortunately, things had just gotten started for the most powerful man in the empire and these bizarre and inhuman acts were only a sampling of what was to come.

Nero was given to fits of rage and became violent towards his wife in one such outburst. He kicked Sabina repeatedly until both she and her unborn child died. Nero is said to have regretted this, and he soon started a hunt for anyone who looked like Sabina, his dead wife. He finally found a slave that is said to have resembled her strongly, and they were married. The catch? The slave was a man. Nero took to dressing him in the clothing of a woman and referring to him as a lady. At this point, Nero’s slippery slope was only getting more slippery. He believed himself to be an artist—a genius, even—and gave massive public performances. If you were in attendance, you could not leave. Why? The doors were locked. Nero also dreamed of singing to his enemies and bringing them to tears for their perceived wrongdoings.

But the emperor was not content with only putting on musical performances. In A.D. 67, he entered into the Olympic Games, which was against the rules (no emperor was allowed to compete in the Games). Nevertheless, Nero entered. He introduced new competitions, such as trumpeting and acting. He entered into several and won each one. His actions caused much outrage since the Olympics were considered a sacred event and Nero had changed them.

However, Nero had an even bigger goal in mind. The chariot races were the biggest spectacle the Olympics had to offer. In them, chariot riders were allowed a team of four horses. Teams would race around a massive arena for a total of seven laps. Sometimes wheels fell off, or chariots crashed into each other. It was not uncommon for drivers to be thrown from their ride and to be trampled to death or to be dragged by their own team of horses. However, the winner would be celebrated and highly paid.

Knowing all the difficulty, danger, and stress involved, you can only imagine how the charioteers felt to see Emperor Nero roll up to the racetrack in an expensive chariot and a team consisting of not four, but ten horses. As it turns out, Nero was inexperienced and out of shape. Almost immediately, he lost control of his team and was thrown from the chariot, being seriously injured in the process. Despite never finishing the race, Nero won first place.

This incident does a good job of demonstrating Nero’s attitude toward his authority at this point in his reign. In fact, in A.D. 66, he won more than 1,800 first-place prizes for his supposed exhibits of artistry. Here was a man that could not be told “no”.

On the night of July 18, A.D. 64, a fire started in Rome’s Circus Maximus. The fire grew and spread, becoming out of control. The fire would rage for the next six days, leaving almost no part of the city untouched. It was devastating for the citizens of Rome and would go on to be the incident Nero would be most widely known for. Many ancient writers blamed Nero for starting the fire, although he was not in the city when it began. Whether or not he started the fire, Nero needed someone to blame. He chose a group of people who were despised and feared by the Romans and tortured them relentlessly. That group was known as the Christians. Tacitus, a secular Roman writer, described it as such, “Nero fastened the guilt and inflicted the most exquisite tortures on a class hated for their abominations, called Christians by the populace. 한 집단의 통치자가 된다는 것은 스트레스와 어려운 결정, 잠 못 이루는 밤들을 수반한다—분명히 정신적으로 약하거나 미성숙한 사람에게 어울리는 자리가 아니다. 보안관이든, 시장이든, 주지사이든, 대통령이든 그 자리는 어렵다. 신경과학 연구에 따르면 평균적인 사람은 25세가 되어야 비로소 완전히 성숙한다고 한다.1 그런데 서기 54년에 겨우 열일곱 살의 통치자가 임명된 일이 있다. 그는 하찮은 판관이나 정치 서기관이 아니었다. 그 소년은 당시 세계에서 가장 큰 제국 가운데 하나의 통치자로 즉위했다. 그 소년의 이름은 네로 클라우디우스 카이사르 아우구스투스 게르마니쿠스—일반적으로 네로라고 불렸다. 그는 로마의 다섯 번째 황제였다.

네로는 시민들의 선거나 선택으로 권력에 오른 것이 아니었다. 그의 어머니 아그리피나는 카이사르 클라우디우스(그녀의 삼촌)와 결혼했고, 클라우디우스는 네로를 아들로 입양했다. 네로는 결국 클라우디우스의 딸 옥타비아와 결혼했는데, 그녀는 네로의 사촌이자 의붓여동생이었다.

서기 54년 10월 13일, 아그리피나는 권세 있는 남편에게 독을 먹여 그를 죽였고, 그녀의 아들 네로가 황제가 되었다. 네로와 그의 어머니가 근친관계에 있었다는 소문이 돌았지만, 새로운 통치자는 신하들에게 호의적으로 받아들여졌고 대중을 기쁘게 하려는 듯 거대한 공공 건물을 명령하고 세금과 식량 가격을 낮추기도 했다. 그러나 그 호의는 오래가지 못했다.

네로는 곧 열네 살의 처남을 죽였고, 이것은 그의 아내를 격노하게 했다. 이 무렵 황제는 해방노예와 관계를 맺고 있었기 때문에 그는 아내를 추방했다. 이것이 여론의 분노를 일으키자 그는 옥타비아가 간통했다는 거짓 혐의로 그녀를 참수하도록 했다.

그는 또한 자신과 결혼하려는 음모를 꾸미던 팝패아 사비나라는 여성에게 집착하게 되었다. 사비나의 부추김으로 네로는 왕좌를 잃을까 두려워 어머니를 죽이기로 결심했다. 계획은 단순했다—아그리피나가 유람선에 있을 때 배를 몰래 침몰시켜 그녀가 익사하게 하는 것이었다. 그러나 일이 뜻대로 되지 않았다. 아그리피나는 수영을 잘해 목숨을 건졌다. 굴하지 않고 네로는 사형 집행자를 보내 대낮에 그녀를 칼로 찔러 죽이게 했다. 유감스럽게도, 제국에서 가장 강력한 사람에게 닥친 일은 이제 막 시작되었을 뿐이며 이러한 기괴하고 비인간적인 행위들은 앞으로 닥칠 일의 단편에 불과했다.

네로는 분노에 사로잡혀 폭력적인 행동을 보였고, 그 한 번의 발작에서 아내에게 폭력을 휘둘렀다. 그는 팝패아를 여러 번 발로 걷어찼고 결국 그녀와 태중의 아이는 죽었다. 네로는 이것을 후회했다고 전해지며 곧 죽은 그의 아내를 닮은 사람을 찾아내려 사냥을 시작했다. 그는 마침내 그녀와 매우 닮았다고 전해지는 노예를 찾아 결혼했다. 문제는 그 노예가 남자였다는 점이다. 네로는 그 남자를 여성의 옷으로 입히고 ‘여인’이라고 불렀다. 이 시점에서 네로의 미끄러운 경사는 더욱 가파르게 기울었다. 그는 자신을 예술가—심지어 천재—로 여겼고 대중 앞에서 거대한 공연을 열었다. 공연장에 있으면 탈 수조차 없었다. 왜냐하면 문이 잠겨 있었기 때문이다. 네로는 또한 적들에게 노래를 불러 그들을 눈물짓게 하고 그들의 잘못을 고백하게 하려는 꿈을 꾸었다.

그러나 황제는 단순히 음악 공연을 여는 데만 만족하지 않았다. 서기 67년, 그는 올림픽 경기대회에 출전했는데 이는 규칙에 어긋나는 일이었다(어떤 황제도 경기대회에 출전할 수 없었다). 그럼에도 불구하고 네로는 출전했다. 그는 나팔 연주나 연기와 같은 새로운 종목들을 도입했고 여러 종목에 참가하여 각각 우승을 차지했다. 그는 올림픽을 신성한 행사로 여겼던 사람들을 분노하게 했다.

그러나 네로에게는 훨씬 더 큰 목표가 있었다. 전차 경주는 올림픽이 제공하는 가장 큰 볼거리였다. 그 경주에서 전차 기수는 네 마리의 말을 팀으로 쓸 수 있었다. 팀은 거대한 경기장을 일주하여 총 일곱 바퀴를 달렸다. 때때로 바퀴가 빠지거나 전차들이 서로 충돌했다. 기수가 전차에서 떨어져 밟혀 죽거나 자신의 말들에게 끌려가 죽는 일도 드물지 않았다. 그러나 승자는 찬양받고 많은 상금을 받았다.

그 모든 어려움과 위험, 스트레스를 아는 사람이라면 전차 기수들이 황제 네로가 값비싼 전차와 네 마리가 아닌 열 마리의 말로 경주장에 나타났을 때 어떤 기분이었을지 상상할 수밖에 없다. 알고 보니 네로는 미숙하고 체력이 부족했다. 거의 즉시 그는 팀을 통제하지 못하고 전차에서 떨어져 심각한 부상을 입었다. 경주를 끝내지 못했음에도 불구하고 네로는 1등을 차지했다.

이 사건은 통치 초기에 네로가 자신의 권위에 대해 어떤 태도를 가졌는지를 잘 보여준다. 사실 서기 66년에는 그는 예술적 전시로 주장되는 것들에 대해 1,800개가 넘는 1등 상을 받았다. 그는 ‘아니오’라는 말을 들을 수 없는 사람이었다.

서기 64년 7월 18일 밤, 로마의 서커스 막시무스에서 화재가 발생했다. 불은 번지고 퍼져 통제 불능이 되었다. 그 불은 다음 여섯 날 동안 맹위를 떨쳐 도시의 거의 모든 지역이 피해를 입었다. 로마 시민들에게는 참혹한 일이었고 네로가 가장 널리 알려지게 된 사건이 되었다. 많은 고대 작가들은 네로가 불을 질렀다고 비난했지만, 그가 불이 시작될 때 도시 안에 있지 않았다는 사실도 있다. 그가 방화를 일으켰는지 여부와 관계없이, 네로는 비난할 대상을 필요로 했다. 그는 로마인들에게 혐오와 두려움의 대상이었던 한 집단을 골라 그들을 가혹하게 고문했다. 그 집단은 기독교인으로 알려져 있었다. 세속적 로마 작가 타키투스는 이렇게 묘사했다. “네로는 그 죄책을 확정하고 그 역겨움으로 미움을 받은 집단, 민중이 그들을 기독교인이라 일컫는 자들에게 가장 지독한 고문을 가했다. 온갖 조롱이 그들의 죽음에 더해졌다. 짐승의 가죽을 덮어 개들에게 찢기게 하여 죽게 하기도 하고, 십자가에 못 박기도 하고, 불에 태워 낮이 다한 뒤 야간의 등불로 삼기도 했다.”

그 사이 네로는 더욱 사악해졌다. 그는 무자비하게 남녀와 어린 기독교인들을 학살했고 점점 더 타락에 빠져들었다. 마침내 서기 68년 6월 9일, 로마 원로원에 의해 공적 적으로 선포된 뒤 로마의 마지막 황제 네로는 스스로 목숨을 끊었다. 그는 겨우 31세였다.

이렇듯 모든 면에서 부패한 사람이 있었다. 그의 생활 방식은 기독교에 깊이 모욕적이었고 그의 박해는 역사상 가장 끔찍한 것들 가운데 하나였다. 우리는 그런 통치자에 대해 어떻게 반응해야 할까? 기독교인들은 그에게 어떻게 반응했는가?

바울은 네로의 치세 아래 살았다. 그는 위에 열거된 모든 끔찍한 일들을 보았다. 그럼에도 불구하고 그는 교회에 다음과 같은 권면을 주었다: 각 사람은 위에 있는 권세들에게 복종하라. 권세는 다 하나님께로서 나지 아니함이 없나니 존재하는 권세들은 다 하나님께서 정하신 바라. 그러므로 권세를 거스르는 자는 하나님의 명을 거스리는 것이니 거스르는 자들은 스스로 정죄를 받으리라. 통치자들은 선한 일을 행하는 자에게는 두려운 자가 아니요 악한 일을 행하는 자에게 두려운 자니 네가 권세를 두려워하지 아니하려거든 선한 일을 하라 그리하면 그로부터 칭찬을 받으리라. 이는 그가 너를 위하여 하나님의 일꾼이 되어 선을 베풀게 하려 함이니라. 만일 악을 행하면 두려워하라 이는 그가 헛되이 칼을 가지지 아니하였음이라 그는 하나님의 일꾼으로서 진노를 집행하는 자니 악을 행하는 자에게 형벌을 내리려 함이라. 그러므로 너희가 진노를 위하여뿐 아니라 양심을 인하여도 복종할지니라—로마서 13:1-5.

이 말씀들은 상황을 고려할 때 불가능하게 보인다. 그럼에도 하나님의 말씀은 우리의 정치적 권세자들이 하나님 자신에 의해 세워진 자들임을 말한다. 얼마나 놀라운 증언인가! 그렇다면 우리는 얼마나 더 우리 권세자들을 존중해야 하는가—비방하지 않고; 가능한 모든 면에서 그들에게 복종하며; 그들의 선거와 캠페인에서 벗어나 있으며; 그러나 최종 판단은 하나님과 그의 권위에 복종해야 하지 않겠는가? 혹은 바울의 표현대로, 각 사람은 위에 있는 권세들에게 복종하라. 권세는 다 하나님께로서 나지 아니함이 없나니…—로마서 13:1.

초대 교회의 신자들은 살인적이고 피에 굶주린 부패한 황제 네로를 하나님께서 정하신 사람으로 보았다. 그들은 그의 권위를 존중하고 공경하려 했으나 궁극적으로는 더 높은 권위인 하나님의 권위에 복종했다. 여기서 우리는 지상 권세들이 ‘하나님의 일꾼’로서 존중하고 순종해야 할 존재라는 가능성 있는 역설을 본다. 그러나 만일 시민 권세가 신자에게 하나님을 거역하라고 요구하는 때가 온다면, 우리는 더 높은 책임을 지닌다—우리는 사람보다 하나님께 순종해야 하리라—사도행전 5:29.

이 모든 것은 점점 더 부패하고 악해져 가는 사회 속에서 살고 있는 우리 신자들에게 큰 책임을 지운다. 우리가 우리의 정부 지도자들을 공경하는 한편 모든 일에서 하나님께 순종하는 그 성경적 균형을 찾을 수 있을까? 아니면 우리가 편안한 삶이 짓밟힌다고 느낄 때 우리 주변의 구원받지 못한 사람들처럼 지상 권세자들의 결점을 헤집어 비난하는 데 실패하는가?

그런즉 너희가 지혜 없는 자 같이 하지 말고 오직 지혜 있는 자 같이 행하여 세월을 아끼라 때가 악하니라. 그런즉 어리석지 말고 오직 주의 뜻이 무엇인가 이해하라—에베소서 5:15-17. 또한 사람이 우리를 그리스도의 일꾼들이요 하나님의 신비를 맡은 집사로 여길지어다. 또 집사들에게 구할 것은 충성이니라—고린도전서 4:2.

우리 각 사람은 거듭난 성경 신봉자로서 삼가 걸으며 세월을 아끼자. 우리는 모두 머지않아 심판대 앞에 서서 정당한 상을 받을 그날에 충성되었다 함을 얻고자 하기 때문이다.

Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb –Exodus 3:1.

The back side of the desert has long been understood as God’s school wherewith He has instructed many of His servants, of whom Moses stands chief. At the prime age of 40, he found himself …learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds. And when he was full forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brethren the children of Israel –Acts 7:22-23.

I have no doubt that God can, and does, use men of great ability, capacity, and training, but spiritual leadership requires an ingredient that is not derived from doing, attaining, and accomplishing. The bane of the zealot is often too little confidence in God and too much confidence in the flesh. This pride and restlessness is not dealt with in a seminary nor is it normally exterminated during vigilant duty. For many of God’s servants, it is extracted from the soul on the soil of deserted sands. This arid and abandoned acreage that appears void of life and fruitfulness is where many servants learn to put their face in the dust and yield to what may seem to be inactivity, unfruitfulness, and rejection.

Moses’ life could be divided into three sections. He spent his first forty years learning the wisdom of Egypt, the next forty as a shepherd in Midian, and a final forty as the shepherd of Israel. We can imagine that the first third of his pilgrimage was filled with tremendous activity, advancement, and accomplishment. It had undoubtedly been rehearsed to him that at his birth he …was exceeding fair, and nourished up in his father’s house three months –Acts 7:20.

The miraculous river rescue by Pharoah’s daughter would serve to confirm that he was destined to be an instrument of God’s divine orchestration. As a centerpiece of national attention, it is certainly understandable how this man who …was mighty in words and in deeds –Acts 7:22, was brimming with self-confidence in his ability to accomplish God’s bidding.

In today’s economy, Moses would be esteemed as the ideal candidate for church leadership. He was in every way qualified. He stood above his countrymen in education, and he possessed above-normal natural, financial, and spiritual endowments. He had emerged from the “University” of Egypt as a man mighty in word and deed and he had an obvious call from God upon his life. He was a conservative man who chose …rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season –Hebrews 11:25.

Still, amidst all his fine credentials he was yet deficient for the work that God had called him to. And so, God conveniently conducted him into the land of Midian to enroll him in another school to feed upon the bitter herbs of disappointment and rejection, obscurity and loneliness, and unfulfilled dreams and longings. While it was his earlier ambition to voluntarily align himself with the people of God, this chapter of his life was enacted by compulsion.

We learn from the account in Exodus that the latter third of his life was loaded with intricate involvement and major ministry. While the exit from Egypt is an exciting read and provides great insight, most of us cannot honestly relate to the mighty Moses and his dynamic coalition with God. Rather, it is the uneventful 40-year mid-section of his life that many of us find ourselves in. Though there are but a few dozen verses that represent these four decades of his life, we assume that it was a thorough schooling that inscribed immense patience, soul searching, and perhaps a bit of frustration.

For us, it represents a period when the parched sands of time about us seem to be producing nothing more fruitful than a revelation of our dry, crusty heart—shriveled and wasted by the consequences of our failures and past sins. It is at these times that we can have a lapse in faith, not that we blame God for our circumstances, but that we may begin to see our lives as futile, and that each day is the same as the previous one. Perhaps we begin to walk around in a visionless stupor—through a fog of spiritual depression—as we grope for encouragement and a reminder that God has not forgotten us. At times, it even seems that our prayers hit the ceiling and bounce back, laughing and lying to us in grim mockery that our usefulness in the Kingdom of God is over. During extended times of trials and testing, we can feel abandoned. We can even imagine that God has turned against us. We look up to Heaven and ask, “Why Lord?” We will never experience rejection and being forsaken to the extent that the Lord Jesus did, but when we experience them in our petty little realm, it seems to sap all our spiritual strength and vigor. We think… If the Lord should require forty years of this from us there would be no time left in our lives to capitalize on what we have learned. But God’s timing is perfect. Thus, it behooves us to not concern ourselves so much with the longevity of our schooling, but to be thoroughly acquainted with the message from Midian. While some receive the bitter strokes of Midian and retreat to stand cynically on the sidelines, we must shake off the dust of the desert and arise with an understanding of…

God’s Purpose

God has a purpose for every detail of our lives. He may plant us in a difficult position, to forge in us a new vocation. It was alone in Midian where Moses learned of his own pride, self-confidence, lack of faith, and the utter folly that his own hands had participated in. Here in his Midian, he was alone and yet not alone; numerous other saints have joined him there. The sons of Jacob and the wife of Potiphar sent another vibrant servant there—Joseph. The wild rage of a jealous king sent a gifted young harpist there. Even an old and foolish king who refused to be taught found himself in a wilderness eating grass like an ox until he recanted of his pride.

Throughout the pages of history, countless saints have realized that ‘the darker the valley, the more I learned to pray’. While they arrive at the threshold of the new day loaded down with bountiful exuberance, they are soon stripped naked in a metamorphic change and finally emerge with nothing but the rod of God in their hands. Gone are the days when they were swift to speak, swift to act, and slow to hear. In Midian, the student learns to shift his focus from, “I will do great things for God” to “What wilt thou have me to do?”

And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do –Acts 9:6. The new arrivals in Midian have many answers, but most of them involve a one-act-play with self as the main character. The graduates walk out silent and sober, for they’ve come through the arduous process of separating the flesh from the spirit which was accomplished by…

God’s Purging

The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts –Proverbs 17:3. As Moses passed through the gates of Midian, the first scene that God set before his eyes was an injustice at a well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters… –Exodus 2:16, who were being driven away by a band of uncouth shepherds. But Moses had been well trained in every dimension of Egyptian plutocracy, which would have included all aspects of military expertise and worldly leadership skills. Thus, when he stepped in to assist the helpless shepherdesses, he would have been quite capable to do so. These daughters of the priest of Midian appreciated the help which they recounted to their father that …An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and also drew water enough for us, and watered the flock –Exodus 2:19. Upon hearing this tale, their father, Reuel, was so impressed that he gave Moses a reception, a job, and a wife… all in one verse. –see Exodus 2:21.

…Ye know that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and their great ones exercise authority upon them –Mark 10:42. While Moses’ quest for justice may have been noble, his orientation was merely Gentile. This may work for establishing pecking order in a hen house, but it is destined for failure in leading forth the people of God. But … whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all –Mark 10:43-44.

This doctrine was foreign to Egypt and to Moses as well. Many good and talented men can successfully operate a business using Gentile authority, but it rarely works in their home, and it is even more futile in a church. Thus, God moved His chosen vessel from royalty to proletariat (the working class), almost overnight. He is then given a job which was loathed by the people who had trained him—…for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians –Genesis 46:34. This fining pot is not just to teach us a much-needed lesson, but to guide us into…

God’s Provision

The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way –Psalm 25:9. God will never abandon us on the back side of the desert; instead, He tailors our life circumstances to bring us into His fullness. If we resist the temptation to espouse an attitude of anger, then God will be able to teach us His ways. But to Moses, the situation presented itself such that God’s divine direction was the last thing he would suspect was happening.

Happening…? It seemed that nothing was happening. The weeks melted into months, the months into years, and the years into decades, all the while the gifted Moses remained an underachieving shepherd. One of the hardest things that we struggle with is “waiting.” Almost every Christian will face a long time of tribulation and we are told to: …think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you –1 Peter 4:12. But we should not judge God’s means by our feeble sense, for in the meantime, the wonderful working of waiting prepares us for…

God’s Promotion

38, 39, … 40 years. Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt –Exodus 3:10.

Perhaps God is enamored with the number 40, but more than likely, it was the time that it took for Moses to land at the seat of resignation. His self-esteem has been fully extinguished, and he humbly asks: …Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh, and that I should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt? –Exodus 3:11.

Moses was not less qualified than he was forty years prior to this time, but his presumption had evaporated in the heat of the desert sun. The experience gleaned in the rugged pastures with the stubborn sheep has brought him to the understanding that this will be nearly an impossible feat. But there is no ordained calling issued independently from…

God’s Promise

…Certainly I will be with thee; and this shall be a token unto thee, that I have sent thee: When thou hast brought forth the people out of Egypt, ye shall serve God upon this mountain –Exodus 3:12.

Not that Moses had attained perfection, for we find Moses provoking God to anger in the very next chapter—And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses… –Exodus 4:14. Then soon again he is the direct object in the path of God’s sword—And it came to pass by the way in the inn, that the LORD met him, and sought to kill him –Exodus 4:24. Even so, while his vessel is still made of clay, it has met with a firing that has prepared him for the Lord’s service, and for us God will not revoke His promises in the wind of our whims. Thus, the great I AM THAT I AM –see Exodus 3:14, has laid upon human shoulders the immense and eternal task of leading His people. But this charge is not to be executed without…

God’s Power

What was the real refinement from Moses’ time spent in the desert? We notice his rash willingness to wield the sword before his arrival, but upon his exit, he only bore a rod in his hand. With the sword he had overcome an Egyptian offender, but with the rod he overcame the entire forces of Egypt. The rod of God brought forth the water in the wilderness. It was the rod of God, that, when lifted high by feeble hands secured the victory over Amalek. What is the rod of God? Before his days in Midian, he hardly knew it existed. Forty years later there hardly exists a scene without it.

The rod is the power of God unto salvation. It is the wisdom of God, the truth of God, the testimony of God, but more than all of these it is the chastening of God. Without it, man does not receive nor perceive the love of God for without it man is not connected to God. For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons –Hebrews 12:6-8.

This same Moses, who at one time was willing to exercise lordship (Gentile authority) over God’s people now finds himself entreating God and staying His wrath from destroying them. The people who accused Moses of leading them out to kill them and even at one point were ready to stone him are now at the center of his heart and affection, even though they are at the cause of his failure to enter the promised land. This is the love of Christ. But where is this learned except under the rod of God, on the back side of the desert, in the Egyptian dungeons, in the caves of Adullam, in the straits of Arabia, and in the silent solitude of the back burner where God has ordained that many of His people go until they learn to …learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls –Matthew 11:29. Surely that is where Moses secured the character known to the biblical scholar as the meekest man to walk the face of the earth. Surely there is no more opposite place on earth to learn it but in the school of suffering.

And so here we shall abide as well, so that we …may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death –Philippians 3:10.

וְעַתָּה מֹשֶׁה שָׁמַר אֶת־צֹאן יִתְרוֹ חֹתֶן־אִישׁ־מִדְיָן וַיַּרְעֶה אֶת־הַצֹּאן אֶל־אַחֲרֹן הַמִּדְבָּר וַיָּבֹא הָר־אֱלֹהִים חֹרֵב – שמות ג:א.

הצד האחורי של המדבר נתפש מזה זמן רב כמסגרת הלימוד של אלוהים שבה הדריך רבים מעבדיו, כאשר משה עומד בראשם. בעשור הראשון של חייו, בגיל ארבעים, מצא את עצמו …חָכָם לְכָל־חָכְמַת מִצְרַיִם וְאִישׁ־הַמַּעֲשִׂים וּבְדְבָרָיו חָזָק וַיְהִי כְּלֵי שְׁלֹשִׁים וּמָאתַיִם בֹּא לִבּוֹ לִבְקֹר אֶת־אֶחָיו בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל – מעשי השליחים ז:כב–כג.

אין לי ספק שאלוהים יכול, ואף עושה, להשתמש באנשי־יכולת רבה, בעלי יכולת והכשרה, אך מנהיגות רוחנית דורשת מרכיב שאינו נובע מעשייה, מהשגה ומהישג. המכשול של הזֶיְלוֹט הוא לעתים חוסר ביטחון מספיק באלהים וביטחון מופרז בבשר. זוהי יהירות וחרמנות שאינה נפתרת בסמינריון ולא נרחקת בדרך כלל בעמל ערני. אצל רבים מעבדיו של אלוהים היא נתלשת מן הנפש על אדמת חולות המדבר הנשכחים. השטח הצחיח והנטוש הזה, שנראה כאילו אין בו חיים ופירות, הוא המקום שבו רבים לומדים לשים את פניהם בעפר ולהיכנע למה שעשוי להיראות כחוסר פעילות, חוסר פריון ודחייה.

חיי משה ניתנים לחלוקה לשלוש תקופות. את ארבעים שנותיו הראשונות בילה בלימוד חכמת מצרים, ארבעים השנים הבאות כרועה במדין, וארבעתים השנים האחרונות כרועה־ישראל. אפשר לדמיין שהשליש הראשון של מסעו היה מלא בפעילות אדירה, בקידום ובהישגים. ללא ספק הוסבר לו שבמועד הולדתו …היה יפה־מראה עד־מאד ונתחלב בבית־אביו שלשה־חודשים – מעשי השליחים ז:כ.

ההצלה הנסית מן הנהר בידי בת פרעה חיזקה את הרושם שהוא נקבע להיות כלי בסדר האלוהי. כמי שהיה במרכז תשומת לב לאומית, מובן מדוע האיש ש…היה חזק בדברים ובמעשים – מעשי השליחים ז:כב, היה מלא ביטחון עצמי ביכולתו למלא את משימת אלוהים.

בכלכלת ימינו, משה היה מוערך כמועמד האידיאלי למנהיגות כנסייתית. בכל דרך היה כשיר. עלה על בני־עמו בחינוך, ובעל יתרונות טבעיים, כלכליים ורוחניים מעל הממוצע. יצא מ"אוניברסיטת" מצרים כאיש־חזק בדבר ובמעשה והיה עליו קריאה בולטת מאלוהים. הוא היה אדם שמרן שבחר …שְׂאֵת לַסַּכִּיּוֹת עִם־עַמּוֹ מִהֲנַגֵּן בְּתַעֲנוּגֵי־הַחֵטְא לְעֵת קָצָה – העברים יא:כה.

עדיין, בין כל הכשירויות הטובות הללו חָסֵר משהו לעבודת הקרא שה' קרא אותו אליה. לכן הוביל אותו אלוהים בנוח את ארץ־מדין, להכניסו לבית־ספר נוסף שבו יאכל מרירות תבלין התאכזבויות ודחייה, חשכת־מעמד ובדידות, וחלומות ותשוקות שלא נשאו פרי. בעוד שבעבר שאף להתיישב בהתנדבות עם עם־אלוהים, פרק זה בחייו הוביל אותו ביד־כפייה.

מוסכם מתוך סיפור שמות שהשליש האחרון של חייו היה עמוס מעורבות מורכבת ומשרתוות עיקריות. היציאה ממצרים מעניינת ומספקת תובנות, אך רובנו לא יכולים באמת להזדהות עם משה הגדול ובעל הברית הדינמית עם אלוהים. במקום זאת, זו ארבעים השנים האמצעיות והבלתי־מרגשות בחייו שבהן רבים מאיתנו מוצאים את עצמם. אף שבהן רק מיעוט פסוקים מייצג תקופה זו של ארבעים שנים, אנו מניחים כי מדובר בבית־ספר יסודי שחרת סבלנות עצומה, חיפוש נפש, ואולי מעט תסכול.

עבורנו, זהו פרק שבו החולות היבשים של הזמן סביבנו נראים כאילו אינן מפיקות יותר מאשר גילוי של לבנו היבש והקשיח—מצומק ומבלוי מתוצאות כשלונותינו וחטאינו שבעבר. בזמנים אלו עלול להתרחש בנו קריסה של אמונה, לא בהאשמת אלוהים על נסיבותינו, אלא בכך שנתחיל לראות את חיינו כחסרי תועלת ושכל יום זהה לקודמו. יתכן שנתחיל לנדוד בתופת חסרת חזון—באובך דיכאון רוחני—נממעים בתקווה וחיפוש עידוד ותזכורת שאלוהים לא שכח אותנו. לפעמים נדמה כי תפילותינו פוגעות בתקרת השמים וחוזרות אלינו בחיוך של לעג, משקרות ומלעיגות לנו כי שימושיותנו בממלכת אלוהים הסתיימה. במשך תקופות ממושכות של ניסיון ובחינה, נוכל להרגיש נטושים. אפילו נדמיין שאלוהים נעצב עלינו. נביט לשמים ונשאל: "למה, אדוני?" לעולם לא נחווה דחייה והושמטות במידה שבה חוו אותם ישוע, אך כאשר אנו חווים אותם בתחום הקטן שלנו, נדמה שהם מוציאים את כל כוחנו ורוחנו הרוחנית. נחשוב… אם ה' ידרוש מאתנו ארבעים שנה כאלה לא יישאר לנו זמן בחיינו לנצל את מה שלמדנו. אך זמנו של אלוהים מושלם. לפיכך ראוי שלא נתעסק כל־כך לאורך ההכשרה, אלא להכיר לעומק את המסר ממדין. בעוד שחלק מדיירי מדין מקבלים את מכת המדין ומסתלקים לעמוד בציניות בשולי הדרך, עלינו לנער מעלינו את אבק המדבר ולקום בהבנה של…

מטרת אלוהים

לאלוהים יש מטרה לכל פרט בחיינו. יתכן שהוא שותל אותנו במיקום קשה כדי לטוות בנו מקצוע חדש. רק במדין למד משה על יהירותו, ביטחונו העצמי, חוסר אמונתו והשׂכל המיותר שבו ידיו היו מעורבות. כאן במדין שלו היה לבד אך לא בודד; קדמוניות רבות הצטרפו אליו שם. בני יעקב ואשת פוטיפר שלחו לשם עוד משרת נאמן—יוסף. זעם פראי של מלך קנאי שלח לשם כנגן כיסא מוכשר. אפילו מלך זקן וטיפש שסירב להינחך מצא את עצמו במדבר אוכל עשב כשור עד שויתר על יהירותו.

במהלך דפי ההיסטוריה גילו אין־ספור קדושים כי ‘‘ככל שהעמק חשוך יותר, כן למדתי להתפלל יותר’’. כשהם מגיעים לסף היום החדש מלאים התלהבות שופעת, הם במהרה נחשפים בעירום בתהליך מטמורפוזה ולבסוף יוצאים עם דבר־אמצע בלבד—מטה אלוהים בידיהם. חלפו הימים שבהם היו מהירים בדבריהם, מהירים במעשיהם ואיטיים בשמיעה. במדין הלומד משנה את מוקד תשומת ליבו מ"אני אעשה דברים גדולים עבור אלוהים" ל"מה תרצה שאעשה?"

וְהוּא רָעֵד וּנִפְתָּא אָמַר אֲדֹנָי מָה־תֶאֱלֶה אָנִי עָשׂוֹת וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו הָאֲדֹנָי קוּם וּבוֹא אֶל־הָעִיר וְנִסַּפֵּר לְךָ אֵת אֲשֶׁר־יְהִי־לָךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת – מעשי השליחים ט:ו. המבקשים החדשים במדין יש להם הרבה תשובות, אך מרביתן כרוכות בהצגה שבה העצמי הוא הדמות הראשית. הבוגרים יוצאים שקטים ורציניים, כי עברו תהליך ארוך של הפרדת הבשר מן הרוח שהושג על־ידי…

טיהורו של אלוהים

כַּד־הַמְּלָחָה לַכֶּסֶף וּתְנּוּר לַזָּהָב וַיהוָה בּוֹחֵן לֵב׃ – משלי יז:ג. כאשר משה עבר את שערי מדין, הסצנה הראשונה שאלוהים הציב מול עיניו הייתה עוולה ליד באר. וַאֲלֵכֶם לְכֹהֵן־מִדְיָן שֶׁבַע בָּנוֹת… – שמות ב:טז, שנדחפו על־ידי כנופיית רועים בוטים. אך משה הוכשר היטב בכל ממדי הפלטוקרטיה המצרית, שכללו גם מיומנויות צבאיות ומיומנויות הנהגה חילוניות. לכן, כשנכנס לעזור לרועות החסרות ישועה, הוא היה בהחלט מסוגל לעשות זאת. בנות הכהן של מדין העריכו את העזרה וסיפרו לאביהן כי …מִצְרִי הִצִּילֵנוּ מִיַּד־הָרוֹעִים וְגַם שָׁלַח לָנוּ־מַיִם־שְׂבֵעַ וַיַּשְׁקוּ אֶת־הַצֹּאן – שמות ב:יט. כששמע את הסיפור התרשם אביהן, רְעוּאֵל, עד שהעניק למשה קבלת פנים, עבודה ואישה… הכל בפסוק אחד. –ראה שמות ב:כא.

…וְאַתֶּם יוֹדְעִים כִּי הָרֹאשִׁים הָעוֹלִים לְמַמְלֵל אֶת־הַגּוֹיִם שָׁלְטוּ בָהֶם וּגְדֹלֵיהֶם הֵטִילו שָׁלִטוֹן עֲלֵיהֶם – מרקוס י:מב. בעוד שחתירתו של משה לצדק יכלה להיות נעלה, כיוונו היה פשוט גוי־לבבי. זה עשוי להתאים לקביעת דרגי כוח בחברת עופות, אך הוא נידון לכשלון בהנהגת עם־אלוהים. וְאַךְ בְּכָל־כֶּן הַרְצוֹן הֵמָּה יִהְיֶה בְּךָ לְגַם לְשִׁירת עֲבֹדָה וּמִי בְכֶם יִרְצֶה לְהִתְפַּאֵר יִהְיֶה עֶבֶד לְכֻלָּם – מרקוס י:מג–מד.

דבר זה היה זר למצרים ולמשה כאחד. אנשים טובים ומוכשרים רבים יכולים לנהל בעסקיות סמכות גוייתית בהצלחה, אך זה נדיר שיעבוד בביתם, וזה חסר תועלת עוד יותר בכנסייה. לכן, הזיז אלוהים את הכלי הנבחר שלו מן המלוכה אל הפרולטריון (מעמד הפועלים), כמעט בן־לילה. אז ניתן לו עבודה שאותה שנאו האנשים שאימנו אותו—…כִּי כָל־רֹעֶה תֹּעֵבָה לְמִצְרָיִם – בראשית מו:לד. כד הכספי הזה אינו רק ללמדנו שיעור נחוץ, אלא להנחותנו אל…

פרנסתו של אלוהים

יַנְחֵם עָנְוִים בְּמִשְׁפָּט וְאֶת־דְּרָכָיו יְלַמֵּד עֲנָוִים – תהלים כה:ט. אלוהים לא יעזוב אותנו בגב המדבר; במקום זאת, הוא מתאים את נסיבות חיינו כדי להביאנו למלאותו. אם נעמוד בפיתוי לאמץ גישה של זעם, אז יוכל אלוהים ללמדנו את דרכיו. אך בעבור משה, המצב הציג את עצמו כך שהדרכה אלוהית תהיה הדבר האחרון שהוא ישער שקורה.

מתרחש…? נדמה כי כלום לא התרחש. השבועות נמסו לחודשים, החודשים לשנים, והשנים לעשורים, וכל הזמן משה המוכשר נשאר רועה כושל. אחת מהדברים הקשים ביותר שאנו נאבקים בהם היא "המתנה". כמעט כל נוצרי יעמוד בתקופה ארוכה של צער ומסופר לנו: …אַל־תֵּסֵסוּ בְּעֵינֵיכֶם עַל־הַמַּסָּה הַלְּכוּת הַמִּתְּעַנֶּכֶת אֶתְכֶם כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּאָה אֵלֵיכֶם – א' פטרוס ד:יב. אך אין לשפוט את דרכי אלוהים לפי תחושתנו החלשה, כי בינתיים, העבודה הנפלאה של ההמתנה מכינה אותנו ל…

קידושו של אלוהים

38, 39, … 40 שנה. עַתָּה לְכָה וְאֶשְׁלְחֻךָ אֶל־פַרְעֹה לְמַעַן תּוֹצִיא אֶת־עַמִּי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרָיִם – שמות ג:י.

אולי אלוהים נמשך למספר ארבעים, אך יש סבירות רבה יותר שזה הזמן שנדרש כדי שמשה יגיע לשלב הויתור. הערך העצמי שלו נכבה עד תום, והוא בפחד שואל: …מִי אָנֹכִי כִי אֵלֵךְ אֶל־פַרְעֹה וְהוֹצֵאתִי אֶת־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרָיִם – שמות ג:יא.

משה לא היה פחות כשיר ממה שהיה לפני ארבעים שנה, אך יומרתו התאדה בחום שמש המדבר. הניסיון שנצבר במרעה המחוספס עם הכבשים העקשניות הביא אותו להבנה שמדובר במשימה כמעט בלתי־אפשרית. אך אין קריאה מוסמכת הניתנת ללא…

הבטחתו של אלוהים

…וְאֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ בְּאֱמֶת וְהָיָה־זֶה לְאוֹת לָךְ כִּי שְׁלַחְתִּיךָ מִצְאתָ אֶת־הָעָם מִמִּצְרָיִם תַּעֲבְדֻנָּה אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים עַל־הָהָר הַזֶּה – שמות ג:יב.

לא כי משה השיג שלמות, שכן אנו מוצאים את משה מעורר את־עֶבֶר ה' כעבור הפרק הבא—וַיִּחַר אַף־יְהוָה בְּמֹשֶׁה… – שמות ד:יד. אז שוב הוא נתפס למרכז חניתה של חרב ה'—וַיְהִי בָדֶרֶךְ בַּמִּלְּחוֹן וַיִּפְגְּשׁוּהוּ יְהוָה וַיְּבַקֵּשׁ לְהַכּוֹתוֹ – שמות ד: כד. אף על־פי כן, כאשר הכלי שלו עדיין עשוי חרס, זה כבר עבר אפייה שהכינה אותו לשרת את־ה', ולנו אלוהים לא יבטל את הבטחותיו ברוח חטפי רצון. לכן, ה"א־היה אשר אֶהְיֶה" –ראה שמות ג:יד, נשא על כתפיים אנושיות את המשימה העצומה והנצחית לערוך את הנהגת עמו. אבל מטלה זו לא תמומש בלא…

כוחו של אלוהים

מה היה השינוי האמיתי מזמן משה במדבר? אנו מבחינים בהכונה הפזיזה שלו להניף חרב לפני בואו, אך ביציאתו החזיק רק מטה בידו. בחרב ניצח עבריין מצרי אחד, אך במטה גבר על כל כוחות מצרים. מטה האלוהים הביא מים במדבר. הוא היה המטה שהניף בידים רפות והביא ניצחון על עמלק. מהו מטה אלוהים? לפני ימיו במדין כמעט שלא ידע שהוא קיים. ארבעים שנה אחר־כך קשה למצוא תמונה בלעדיו.

המטה הוא כוחו של אלוהים אל־הישועה. הוא חכמת אלוהים, אמת אלוהים, עדות אלוהים, אך יותר מכל אלה הוא תקון ואילוף האלוהים. בלעדיו האדם אינו מקבל ולא תופס את אהבת אלוהים, כי בלעדיו האדם אינו קשור לאלוהים. כִּי אֲשֶׁר־יֶאֱהַב יְהוָה יוֹכַח וְיוֹכִח כָּל־בֵּן אֲשֶׁר־קִבֵּל וְאִם־תְּאָבְלוּ תּוֹכַח אֱלֹהִים אֶתְכֶם כְּבָנִים כִּי־מִי הָאֲשֶׁר־הוּא בֵּן אֲשֶׁר אֵינֶנּוּ הוּא מוּכָח׃ וְאִם־אֲתֶם בְּלִי־מוּכָח אֵלּוּ אֲשֶׁר־הֶחֱלִיקוּ עֹרֶךְ יֵשְׁרוּ אַחֲרֵיהֶם אֵין־הֵם בָּנִים – העברים יב:ו–ח.

אותו משה, שבעת־יד אחת היה נוטה לנהוג בשלטון (סמכות גוייתית) על עמי־אלוהים, מוצא את עצמו כעת מתחנן בפני ה' ומעצור את זעמו מלַשְׁמֹדם. האנשים שהאשימו את משה כי הוציאם למות ואפילו היו על סף לקבור אותו באבנים נמצאים כעת בלבו ובחיבתו, אף על־פי שהם הסיבה לכישלו להיכנס אל הארץ המובטחת. זו אהבת המשיח. אך היכן לומדים זאת אם לא תחת מטה האלוהים, בגב המדבר, בבורות המצריים, במערות עדולם, בחרפות ערב וסביב בדידות השקט שבה ה' קבע שרבים מעמו ילכו עד שלמדו …לִמְדוּ מִמֶּנִּי כִּי עָנָו וּמְצָנֵעַ לֵב וּמְצָא תְּנוּחָה לְנַפְשׁוֹתֵיכֶם – מתי יא:כט. ודאי שם השיג משה את האופי שהמלומד המקראי מכנה את־אישיותו כאדם העניו ביותר שפסע על פני הארץ. אין ודאי מקום עיקרי נגדי ללמוד זאת אלא בבית־ספר הסבל.

ולכן גם אנחנו נשהה כאן, כדי שנספיק …לָדַעַת אֹתוֹ וְאֶת־כֹּחַ תְּחִיָּתוֹ וְאֶת־תַּחְבֻּרוּת מַעֲנָיוֹתָיו וְנִהְיֶה כְּמוֹתָיו בְּמָוֶת – פיליפים ג:י.

Now Moses kept the flock of Jethro his father-in-law, the priest of Midian: and he led the flock to the backside of the desert, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb –Exodus 3:1.

The back side of the desert has long been understood as God’s school wherewith He has instructed many of His servants, of whom Moses stands chief. At the prime age of 40, he found himself …learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds. And when he was full forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brethren the children of Israel –Acts 7:22-23.

I have no doubt that God can, and does, use men of great ability, capacity, and training, but spiritual leadership requires an ingredient that is not derived from doing, attaining, and accomplishing. The bane of the zealot is often too little confidence in God and too much confidence in the flesh. This pride and restlessness is not dealt with in a seminary nor is it normally exterminated during vigilant duty. For many of God’s servants, it is extracted from the soul on the soil of deserted sands. This arid and abandoned acreage that appears void of life and fruitfulness is where many servants learn to put their face in the dust and yield to what may seem to be inactivity, unfruitfulness, and rejection.

Moses’ life could be divided into three sections. He spent his first forty years learning the wisdom of Egypt, the next forty as a shepherd in Midian, and a final forty as the shepherd of Israel. We can imagine that the first third of his pilgrimage was filled with tremendous activity, advancement, and accomplishment. It had undoubtedly been rehearsed to him that at his birth he …was exceeding fair, and nourished up in his father’s house three months –Acts 7:20.

The miraculous river rescue by Pharoah’s daughter would serve to confirm that he was destined to be an instrument of God’s divine orchestration. As a centerpiece of national attention, it is certainly understandable how this man who …was mighty in words and in deeds –Acts 7:22, was brimming with self-confidence in his ability to accomplish God’s bidding.

In today’s economy, Moses would be esteemed as the ideal candidate for church leadership. He was in every way qualified. He stood above his countrymen in education, and he possessed above-normal natural, financial, and spiritual endowments. He had emerged from the “University” of Egypt as a man mighty in word and deed and he had an obvious call from God upon his life. He was a conservative man who chose …rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season –Hebrews 11:25.

Still, amidst all his fine credentials he was yet deficient for the work that God had called him to. And so, God conveniently conducted him into the land of Midian to enroll him in another school to feed upon the bitter herbs of disappointment and rejection, obscurity and loneliness, and unfulfilled dreams and longings. While it was his earlier ambition to voluntarily align himself with the people of God, this chapter of his life was enacted by compulsion.

We learn from the account in Exodus that the latter third of his life was loaded with intricate involvement and major ministry. While the exit from Egypt is an exciting read and provides great insight, most of us cannot honestly relate to the mighty Moses and his dynamic coalition with God. Rather, it is the uneventful 40-year mid-section of his life that many of us find ourselves in. Though there are but a few dozen verses that represent these four decades of his life, we assume that it was a thorough schooling that inscribed immense patience, soul searching, and perhaps a bit of frustration.

For us, it represents a period when the parched sands of time about us seem to be producing nothing more fruitful than a revelation of our dry, crusty heart—shriveled and wasted by the consequences of our failures and past sins. It is at these times that we can have a lapse in faith, not that we blame God for our circumstances, but that we may begin to see our lives as futile, and that each day is the same as the previous one. Perhaps we begin to walk around in a visionless stupor—through a fog of spiritual depression—as we grope for encouragement and a reminder that God has not forgotten us. At times, it even seems that our prayers hit the ceiling and bounce back, laughing and lying to us in grim mockery that our usefulness in the Kingdom of God is over. During extended times of trials and testing, we can feel abandoned. We can even imagine that God has turned against us. We look up to Heaven and ask, “Why Lord?” We will never experience rejection and being forsaken to the extent that the Lord Jesus did, but when we experience them in our petty little realm, it seems to sap all our spiritual strength and vigor. We think… If the Lord should require forty years of this from us there would be no time left in our lives to capitalize on what we have learned. But God’s timing is perfect. Thus, it behooves us to not concern ourselves so much with the longevity of our schooling, but to be thoroughly acquainted with the message from Midian. While some receive the bitter strokes of Midian and retreat to stand cynically on the sidelines, we must shake off the dust of the desert and arise with an understanding of…

God’s Purpose

God has a purpose for every detail of our lives. He may plant us in a difficult position, to forge in us a new vocation. It was alone in Midian where Moses learned of his own pride, self-confidence, lack of faith, and the utter folly that his own hands had participated in. Here in his Midian, he was alone and yet not alone; numerous other saints have joined him there. The sons of Jacob and the wife of Potiphar sent another vibrant servant there—Joseph. The wild rage of a jealous king sent a gifted young harpist there. Even an old and foolish king who refused to be taught found himself in a wilderness eating grass like an ox until he recanted of his pride.

Throughout the pages of history, countless saints have realized that ‘the darker the valley, the more I learned to pray’. While they arrive at the threshold of the new day loaded down with bountiful exuberance, they are soon stripped naked in a metamorphic change and finally emerge with nothing but the rod of God in their hands. Gone are the days when they were swift to speak, swift to act, and slow to hear. In Midian, the student learns to shift his focus from, “I will do great things for God” to “What wilt thou have me to do?”

And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise, and go into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do –Acts 9:6. The new arrivals in Midian have many answers, but most of them involve a one-act-play with self as the main character. The graduates walk out silent and sober, for they’ve come through the arduous process of separating the flesh from the spirit which was accomplished by…

God’s Purging

The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts –Proverbs 17:3. As Moses passed through the gates of Midian, the first scene that God set before his eyes was an injustice at a well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters… –Exodus 2:16, who were being driven away by a band of uncouth shepherds. But Moses had been well trained in every dimension of Egyptian plutocracy, which would have included all aspects of military expertise and worldly leadership skills. Thus, when he stepped in to assist the helpless shepherdesses, he would have been quite capable to do so. These daughters of the priest of Midian appreciated the help which they recounted to their father that …An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and also drew water enough for us, and watered the flock –Exodus 2:19. Upon hearing this tale, their father, Reuel, was so impressed that he gave Moses a reception, a job, and a wife… all in one verse. –see Exodus 2:21.

…Ye know that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and their great ones exercise authority upon them –Mark 10:42. While Moses’ quest for justice may have been noble, his orientation was merely Gentile. This may work for establishing pecking order in a hen house, but it is destined for failure in leading forth the people of God. But … whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all –Mark 10:43-44.

This doctrine was foreign to Egypt and to Moses as well. Many good and talented men can successfully operate a business using Gentile authority, but it rarely works in their home, and it is even more futile in a church. Thus, God moved His chosen vessel from royalty to proletariat (the working class), almost overnight. He is then given a job which was loathed by the people who had trained him—…for every shepherd is an abomination unto the Egyptians –Genesis 46:34. This fining pot is not just to teach us a much-needed lesson, but to guide us into…

God’s Provision

The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way –Psalm 25:9. God will never abandon us on the back side of the desert; instead, He tailors our life circumstances to bring us into His fullness. If we resist the temptation to espouse an attitude of anger, then God will be able to teach us His ways. But to Moses, the situation presented itself such that God’s divine direction was the last thing he would suspect was happening.

Happening…? It seemed that nothing was happening. The weeks melted into months, the months into years, and the years into decades, all the while the gifted Moses remained an underachieving shepherd. One of the hardest things that we struggle with is “waiting.” Almost every Christian will face a long time of tribulation and we are told to: …think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you –1 Peter 4:12. But we should not judge God’s means by our feeble sense, for in the meantime, the wonderful working of waiting prepares us for…

God’s Promotion

38, 39, … 40 years. Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt –Exodus 3:10.

Perhaps God is enamored with the number 40, but more than likely, it was the time that it took for Moses to land at the seat of resignation. His self-esteem has been fully extinguished, and he humbly asks: …Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh, and that I should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt? –Exodus 3:11.

Moses was not less qualified than he was forty years prior to this time, but his presumption had evaporated in the heat of the desert sun. The experience gleaned in the rugged pastures with the stubborn sheep has brought him to the understanding that this will be nearly an impossible feat. But there is no ordained calling issued independently from…

God’s Promise

…Certainly I will be with thee; and this shall be a token unto thee, that I have sent thee: When thou hast brought forth the people out of Egypt, ye shall serve God upon this mountain –Exodus 3:12.

Not that Moses had attained perfection, for we find Moses provoking God to anger in the very next chapter—And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses… –Exodus 4:14. Then soon again he is the direct object in the path of God’s sword—And it came to pass by the way in the inn, that the LORD met him, and sought to kill him –Exodus 4:24. Even so, while his vessel is still made of clay, it has met with a firing that has prepared him for the Lord’s service, and for us God will not revoke His promises in the wind of our whims. Thus, the great I AM THAT I AM –see Exodus 3:14, has laid upon human shoulders the immense and eternal task of leading His people. But this charge is not to be executed without…

God’s Power

What was the real refinement from Moses’ time spent in the desert? We notice his rash willingness to wield the sword before his arrival, but upon his exit, he only bore a rod in his hand. With the sword he had overcome an Egyptian offender, but with the rod he overcame the entire forces of Egypt. The rod of God brought forth the water in the wilderness. It was the rod of God, that, when lifted high by feeble hands secured the victory over Amalek. What is the rod of God? Before his days in Midian, he hardly knew it existed. Forty years later there hardly exists a scene without it.

The rod is the power of God unto salvation. It is the wisdom of God, the truth of God, the testimony of God, but more than all of these it is the chastening of God. Without it, man does not receive nor perceive the love of God for without it man is not connected to God. For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. If ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons –Hebrews 12:6-8.

This same Moses, who at one time was willing to exercise lordship (Gentile authority) over God’s people now finds himself entreating God and staying His wrath from destroying them. The people who accused Moses of leading them out to kill them and even at one point were ready to stone him are now at the center of his heart and affection, even though they are at the cause of his failure to enter the promised land. This is the love of Christ. But where is this learned except under the rod of God, on the back side of the desert, in the Egyptian dungeons, in the caves of Adullam, in the straits of Arabia, and in the silent solitude of the back burner where God has ordained that many of His people go until they learn to …learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls –Matthew 11:29. Surely that is where Moses secured the character known to the biblical scholar as the meekest man to walk the face of the earth. Surely there is no more opposite place on earth to learn it but in the school of suffering.

And so here we shall abide as well, so that we …may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, being made conformable unto his death –Philippians 3:10.
